questions.q: What does DBCC CHECKDB actually validate?
options: The logical and physical integrity of every object in the database — allocation, page structure, index/table consistency
Only login permissions
Only whether backups exist
Only whether statistics are up to date
questions.explain: CHECKDB is the comprehensive corruption-detection check across the whole database, not a permissions or statistics tool.

questions.q: Why must integrity checks be scheduled rather than run reactively when something seems wrong?
options: SQL Server doesn't proactively surface corruption, so it can sit undetected and get carried into every subsequent backup
DBCC CHECKDB can only be run once per database, ever
Reactive checks are actually faster than scheduled ones
SQL Server automatically repairs corruption the moment it happens
questions.explain: A corrupt page can go unnoticed until a query touches it, by which point it may already be baked into recent backups — scheduling catches it earlier.

questions.q: What does WITH PHYSICAL_ONLY do differently from a full DBCC CHECKDB run?
options: It's a faster subset check for storage-level corruption, skipping the full logical consistency pass
It checks logins and permissions instead of data pages
It automatically repairs any corruption found
It only works on databases in SIMPLE recovery model
questions.explain: PHYSICAL_ONLY catches torn pages and checksum failures faster, without the full logical consistency checks a complete CHECKDB run performs.

questions.q: For a multi-terabyte database that can't finish a nightly full CHECKDB in its maintenance window, what's a realistic alternative mentioned in this lesson?
options: Run a weekly full CHECKDB with PHYSICAL_ONLY checks between, or restore the backup to a separate server and check it there
Never run CHECKDB and rely entirely on backups
Disable AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS instead
Switch the database to SIMPLE recovery model
questions.explain: Weekly full CHECKDB plus PHYSICAL_ONLY on other nights, or offloading the check to a restored copy on another server, are the realistic tradeoffs for very large databases.

questions.q: If DBCC CHECKDB finds corruption, what does this lesson say is almost always the better answer compared to a repair option?
options: Restoring from a known-good backup taken before the corruption occurred
Running REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS immediately without evaluating alternatives
Ignoring the finding since CHECKDB self-corrects over time
Dropping and recreating the entire database
questions.explain: Repair options can themselves cost data; restoring from a known-good backup is generally the safer, more predictable recovery path.
